doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Metaphysics, her grandmother, and reading
summary: She describes her interest in metaphysics, her grandmother the metaphysician, watching toddler programs, and what she reads.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: You have any kind of spiritual connection with your music?
Well I’ve always been like into metaphysics, and it wasn’t until after my grandmother died that they finally told me she was a metaphysician.
You know you’re going to have to explain what you mean by that for me.

Metaphysicians? That’s somebody who does, the visualize, they can image certain things, either for themself or someone else, and the thing will take place. And it could be something really bizarre. But if they get the feeling of it and they can see it, it happens. So I think I just picked that up from my grandmother without even knowing. So I do a lot of things in that way without even knowing, expecting everyone to understand what I’m doing and how I’m doing it. And I think little kids, that’s why I feel really close with little kids, because they can do that. I’m always looking at them. Even the little kids, on Channel 13, the little kiddies program, they hardly even talk, so it’s got to be like one year old. They’ve got a program for little kids. And I’m like ten minutes watching this program. I don’t know there’s something, it’s nonverbal but it’s very, very definite, and it brings results in the visible world. So I love things like that. That’s one of my hobbies.
What kind of reading do you like to do?
That’s a big part of it?
That would be it. That it would just be mostly. I like some biographies too, but if someone comes up with something I’ll read it. I don’t go searching for things. There’s so many things to do.
I know you’ve already said that this is the time for you. In New York, this is the time.
I can’t say — ten years from now I might think it’s even more or less, but—
